source_refs.note: Chapter 13 exercise (PDF 10-11), solved: 8 MCQs keyed from the chapter's text, 4 short questions (Q4 six pairs as tables), 7 long and 3 inquisitive questions with model answers. No answer key is printed.

blocks.prompt: 1. Which term covers the rest of the three?
blocks.explanation: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a stable internal environment; its important processes are thermoregulation, osmoregulation and excretion (13.1).

blocks.prompt: 2. Marine fishes compensate for water loss by:
blocks.explanation: Marine fishes are hypotonic to seawater and lose water by osmosis; to compensate they drink seawater continuously and make small amounts of concentrated urine (13.2.2).

blocks.prompt: 3. How do freshwater fish primarily gain water?
blocks.explanation: Freshwater fish are hypertonic to their surroundings, so water continuously enters by osmosis, especially across the gills; they rarely drink water (13.2.2).

blocks.prompt: 4. What is the primary heat source for endotherms?
blocks.explanation: Endotherms (birds and mammals) generate most of their body heat through internal metabolism (13.3.1).

blocks.prompt: 5. What is the control center for human thermoregulation?
blocks.explanation: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat; it receives signals from skin thermoreceptors, has its own thermoreceptors and sends signals to muscles and glands (13.3.2, 13.3.3).

blocks.prompt: 6. Which waste product requires the most water for excretion?
blocks.explanation: One gram of ammonia needs 500 mL of water to dilute it to a non-toxic level, urea 50 mL and uric acid only 1 mL (13.2.3).

blocks.prompt: 7. Which nitrogenous waste is the least toxic and water-insoluble?
blocks.explanation: Uric acid is even less toxic than urea; it is poorly soluble in water and forms precipitates, needing just 1 mL of water per gram (13.2.3).

blocks.prompt: 8. In which part of the body, the conversion of ammonia to urea takes place?
blocks.explanation: Terrestrial animals convert ammonia into urea in the liver and then excrete urea through the kidneys (13.2.3).

blocks.prompt: 1. Define osmoregulators and osmoconformers.
blocks.explanation:
Osmoregulators: animals that regulate the concentration of water and solutes in their body fluids and keep it constant despite changes in the environment, e.g. most aquatic and terrestrial vertebrates.
Osmoconformers: animals that allow the osmotic concentration of their body fluids to match the environment (isotonic to it), e.g. marine invertebrates, hagfishes, sharks and rays.

blocks.prompt: 2. Define thermoregulation and explain its needs.
blocks.explanation:
Thermoregulation is the homeostatic process by which organisms keep their internal body temperature within a tolerable range, whatever the outside temperature.
Need: enzymes work best at an optimal temperature; below it the metabolic rate drops, well above it enzymes denature. Cell membranes lose selective permeability when hot and become rigid and brittle when cold.

blocks.prompt: 3. What are the two types of animals on the basis of the ability to thermoregulate?
blocks.explanation:
1. Poikilotherms: cannot keep body temperature within narrow limits; it varies with the environment, e.g. invertebrates, fishes, amphibians, reptiles.
2. Homeotherms: keep a relatively constant body temperature whatever the environment, using the hypothalamus as thermostat, e.g. birds and mammals.

blocks.prompt: 1. Describe three elements which operate homeostatic mechanisms.
blocks.explanation:
Homeostasis is maintained by the collaboration of three elements: receptors, control centre and effectors.
1. Receptors (sensors): specialized organs, tissues, cells or subcellular parts that detect changes in the internal or external environment and send this information to the control centre. E.g. receptor cells in the skin detect temperature changes; receptor cells in blood vessels detect changes in blood pressure.
2. Control centre: receives the information from receptors, processes it and sends suitable messages to the effectors, so that the internal environment stays within a narrow range of set points (optimal for body function). The brain, spinal cord and endocrine glands act as control centres.
3. Effectors: parts that respond to the messages of the control centre. Muscles respond by contracting and glands by releasing secretions; the responses bring the internal environment back to its set point.
Example: when body temperature drops below the set point, the effectors in skin and muscles cause shivering and vasoconstriction; heat production rises and the temperature returns to the set point.
Sequence: change (stimulus) -> receptor -> control centre -> effector -> response -> set point restored.

blocks.prompt: 2. Relate the homeostatic mechanisms with the negative and positive feedback systems.
blocks.explanation:
Feedback mechanisms are the foundations of homeostasis: regulatory processes in which the output (product) of a system is used to control the behaviour of the system itself.
Negative feedback:
1. The output reduces the activity of the system; it is the most common form of regulation.
2. Examples: regulation of body temperature, blood glucose level and hormone secretion.
3. Body temperature: if it exceeds the set point of 37°C, thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect it and signal the control centre (thermoregulator in the hypothalamus). The control centre sends messages to effectors (sweat glands), which produce sweat and lower the temperature. The lowered temperature acts negatively on the thermoreceptors, so they stop sending messages; the correction stops at the set point.
Positive feedback:
1. The output increases the activity of the system and so enhances the original stimulus; less common in homeostasis.
2. It occurs in processes that need rapid and large changes, e.g. blood clotting, labour and childbirth.
3. Childbirth: contractions of the uterus send nerve impulses to the control centre (part of hypothalamus); it signals the pituitary gland to release oxytocin; oxytocin causes stronger contractions, which send more impulses and cause more oxytocin release. The loop continues until the baby is born.
Unregulated positive feedback can cause health problems, e.g. in severe inflammation or infection immune cells release cytokines that further stimulate the immune response; if unchecked, this leads to excessive inflammation and tissue damage.
Relation: negative feedback keeps conditions stable around the set point (most homeostasis), while positive feedback drives a process quickly to completion and must be stopped by an end event.

blocks.prompt: 3. Explain the different methods of osmoregulation found in freshwater, marine water and terrestrial habitats.
blocks.explanation:
Osmoregulation is the maintenance of the balance of water and solutes in the body fluids.
1. Freshwater animals:
Problem: they are hypertonic to their environment (higher solute concentration in body fluids). Water continuously enters by osmosis, especially across permeable surfaces like gills, and salts (Na+, Cl-) diffuse out.
Methods: they prevent water entry and eliminate the excess water by producing large volumes of dilute urine; they actively transport salts back into the body; they rarely drink water.
2. Marine animals:
Problem: most are hypotonic to sea water. Water constantly leaves through the gills and skin by osmosis, and salts diffuse in; drinking sea water adds more salt.
Methods: they drink sea water continuously to replace water; they conserve water by producing very small amounts of highly concentrated urine; chloride cells in the gills use ATP to pump salts out actively; kidneys remove excess salts; some marine fishes have rectal glands that remove salts into the digestive tract, eliminated with faeces.
3. Terrestrial animals:
Problem: water is lost by evaporation from respiratory surfaces and skin and in excretion; water intake (drinking, food) and metabolic water must equal the loss.
Methods:
a. Relatively impermeable outer layers: waxy chitin exoskeleton of insects, keratin scales of reptiles, dead keratinized skin cells and oil glands of birds and mammals.
b. Kidneys retain water; ammonia is converted into urea or uric acid, which need less water for excretion.
c. Behaviour: many desert animals stay underground during the heat of the day and come out at night; they feed on carbohydrate-rich seeds; the kangaroo rat survives entirely on metabolic water.
d. Anhydrobiosis: tardigrades (water bears) lose almost all body water, become dormant and revive years later when water returns.

blocks.prompt: 4. Explain the nature of nitrogenous wastes in relation to habitat.
blocks.explanation:
In many animals osmoregulation is coupled with removal of metabolic wastes. The main nitrogenous wastes are ammonia, urea and uric acid; they are excreted as water solutes, and the form depends on how much water the habitat provides.
1. Ammonia (NH3): formed in the liver when the amino group (-NH2) removed from amino acids and nucleic acids combines with H+. It is highly toxic and must be excreted rapidly; 1 g needs 500 mL of water. Only aquatic animals with plenty of water can afford it, e.g. most fishes, protozoans, sponges, coelenterates; they excrete it directly into the water. Such animals are ammonotelic.
2. Urea, CO(NH2)2: terrestrial animals must conserve water and cannot excrete ammonia. They convert ammonia to urea in the liver and excrete it through the kidneys. Urea is less toxic; 1 g needs 50 mL of water. Such animals are ureotelic, e.g. humans. Humans also excrete a small amount of uric acid (from purine breakdown in the liver); excess uric acid in blood forms crystals in joints and causes gout.
3. Uric acid, C5H4N4O3: insects, desert animals, birds and most reptiles face extreme water shortage and cannot afford even urea. They convert ammonia to uric acid using a lot of energy. It is even less toxic, less soluble, forms precipitates and needs just 1 mL of water per gram. Such animals are uricotelic.
Conclusion: the less water available in the habitat, the less toxic and less water-demanding the waste.

blocks.prompt: 5. Classify animals on the basis of the source of body's heat.
blocks.explanation:
On the basis of the source of body heat, animals are ectotherms and endotherms.
1. Ectotherms:
- Gain most of their body heat from external sources; internal temperature generally fluctuates with the surroundings.
- Metabolic rate is very low; they cannot produce enough heat to raise and keep their body temperature, so they rely on environmental heat.
- They use behavioural thermoregulation: when too cold they bask in the sun (radiation) or sit on a warm rock (conduction); when too hot they seek shade or burrow into cool earth; in very cold climates they become dormant in the coldest months.
- Examples: most invertebrates; among vertebrates fishes, amphibians and reptiles.
2. Endotherms:
- Generate most of their body heat by internal metabolism; keep a relatively constant body temperature, often higher than the environment.
- In cold they shiver (muscle contractions) or burn brown adipose tissue for heat.
- Most have insulation to retain heat: hair, feathers or fat.
- Examples: birds and mammals.

blocks.prompt: 6. Classify the animals on the bases of the ability to thermoregulate.
blocks.explanation:
On the basis of the ability to thermoregulate, animals are poikilotherms and homeotherms.
1. Poikilotherms:
- Unable to keep body temperature within narrow limits; it varies considerably, usually matching the temperature of the environment.
- Examples: all invertebrates; among vertebrates fishes, amphibians and reptiles.
- Advantage: they do not need to eat massive amounts of food to 'fuel' a constant temperature, so they can survive in nutrient-poor environments where a homeotherm would starve.
2. Homeotherms:
- Keep a relatively constant internal body temperature regardless of environmental changes.
- They use a 'thermostat' (hypothalamus in the brain) to trigger cooling or heating responses.
- Examples: mammals and birds; humans keep about 37°C in very cold or very hot environments.

blocks.prompt: 7. Describe the regulatory strategies in man for thermoregulation.
blocks.explanation:
Humans are endothermic homeotherms; they regulate body temperature (about 37°C) by negative feedback.
Mechanism: thermoreceptors in the skin detect a rise or fall in temperature and send signals to the control centre, the hypothalamus (which also has thermoreceptors for blood temperature). The hypothalamus signals muscles and glands, which produce corrective responses.
1. Responses to overheating (hyperthermia, above 37°C):
a. Vasodilation: the vessels (arterioles) supplying the skin capillaries just beneath the epidermis widen; more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost.
b. Sweating: evaporation of sweat carries heat away and cools the body.
c. The thyroid gland may decrease thyroxine secretion, lowering the basal metabolic rate and internal heat production.
2. Responses to cooling (hypothermia, below 37°C):
a. Vasoconstriction: less blood flows to the skin, so less heat is lost.
b. Shivering: spasmodic contraction of skeletal muscles produces heat.
c. Goosebumps: tiny muscles at the base of hair follicles contract; air trapped in the erect hair insulates.
d. Increased metabolic rate produces more heat.
3. Behavioural responses: thermoreceptors also stimulate the higher centres of the brain, so we 'feel' warmth or cold and act, e.g. taking a bath or turning fans or heaters on.
When the temperature returns to the set point, the receptors stop signalling (negative feedback).

blocks.prompt: 1. Why positive feedback mechanisms in humans are sometimes associated with severe health problems?
blocks.explanation:
In positive feedback the output increases the activity of the system and enhances the original stimulus, so the change keeps growing instead of being corrected.
Normally the loop is stopped by an end event (e.g. birth of the baby ends the oxytocin loop; a clot sealing the wound ends clotting).
If it is not properly regulated, the response grows out of control. Example from the chapter: in severe inflammation or infection, immune cells release cytokines that further stimulate the immune response; unchecked, this causes excessive inflammation and tissue damage.
Other examples (beyond the chapter): uncontrolled clotting can block vessels (thrombosis); a very high fever raises metabolism, which raises temperature further.

blocks.prompt: 2. List some of the behavioural responses of the animals to maintain homeostasis.
blocks.explanation:
From the chapter:
1. Ectotherms bask in the sun or sit on warm rocks when cold.
2. They seek shade or burrow into cool earth when hot.
3. In very cold climates they become dormant in the coldest months.
4. Desert animals stay underground in the heat of the day and come out at night when the air is cool and humid.
5. Desert animals feed on carbohydrate-rich seeds (metabolic water); marine animals drink sea water, while freshwater animals rarely drink.
6. Humans take a bath or turn on fans or heaters when they feel warm or cold.
Beyond the chapter: dogs pant; elephants flap their ears; birds fluff feathers; penguins huddle; animals migrate to warmer places; humans wear warm or light clothes.

blocks.prompt: 3. Draw a flow chart to show negative feedback of homeostatic mechanisms by taking an example of hormone.
blocks.explanation:
Example: control of blood glucose by insulin (the hormone example is beyond the chapter; the chapter names hormone secretion as a negative feedback). Draw these boxes joined by arrows, ending with an arrow back to the start:
1. Stimulus: blood glucose rises above the set point (after a meal).
2. Receptor: cells of the pancreas (islets of Langerhans) detect the rise.
3. Control centre: the pancreas releases the hormone insulin into the blood.
4. Effectors: liver and muscle cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
5. Response: blood glucose falls back to the set point.
6. Negative feedback arrow (marked '-'): the normal glucose level reduces insulin secretion, so the loop switches off.
(A second loop can be added for low glucose: glucagon -> liver releases glucose -> glucose rises to the set point.)
